q: Who discovered the cell in 1665 while examining a thin slice of cork?
x: Robert Hooke saw box-like compartments in cork under his microscope and named them cells, after the small rooms of a monastery. Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living cells.
e: Hooke saw dead cork cells; Leeuwenhoek saw living ones.

q: Which cell organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
x: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration and release energy as ATP, which is why they are called the powerhouse of the cell. They have their own DNA.
e: Mitochondria make ATP; ribosomes make protein; lysosomes digest.

q: The nucleus of the cell was discovered by whom?
x: Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells. He is also remembered for Brownian motion.
e: Robert Brown: nucleus and Brownian motion.

q: The double helix structure of DNA was proposed in 1953 by whom?
x: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix in 1953, using X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.
e: Two strands, twisted — Watson and Crick, 1953.

q: How many bones are there in the body of an adult human being?
x: An adult human skeleton has 206 bones. A newborn has around 300, many of which fuse together as the child grows.
e: Baby about 300, adult 206 — bones fuse as you grow.

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
x: The human heart has four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. The right side pumps blood to the lungs and the left side pumps it to the rest of the body.
e: Four chambers: two atria receive, two ventricles pump; the left ventricle has the thickest wall.

q: Which is the smallest bone in the human body?
x: The stapes, or stirrup bone, in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the body. The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest.
e: Smallest stapes in the ear; longest femur in the thigh.

q: Insulin is secreted by which organ?
x: The beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose. A shortage of it causes diabetes mellitus.
e: Pancreas: insulin lowers sugar, glucagon raises it.

q: Human blood groups were discovered by whom?
x: Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood group system in 1901 and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1930. He later helped identify the Rh factor.
e: Landsteiner ABO; Harvey described blood circulation.

q: Malaria is transmitted by the bite of which organism?
x: The female Anopheles mosquito transmits the Plasmodium parasite that causes malaria. Aedes aegypti spreads dengue and chikungunya.
e: Anopheles malaria, Aedes dengue, Culex filaria.

q: The deficiency of which vitamin causes scurvy?
x: Scurvy, with bleeding gums and slow healing, comes from a shortage of vitamin C, or ascorbic acid, found in citrus fruits and amla.
e: A night blindness, B1 beriberi, C scurvy, D rickets, K poor clotting.

q: Goitre is caused by the deficiency of which element in the diet?
x: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine. Without enough of it the thyroid gland enlarges, which is goitre. Iodised salt is the common remedy.
e: Iodine for the thyroid; iron for haemoglobin.

q: Which vitamin is needed for the normal clotting of blood?
x: Vitamin K is needed to make several clotting factors in the liver. Its deficiency leads to prolonged bleeding.
e: K for koagulation — the German spelling that gave the vitamin its letter.

q: The green pigment in plants that captures sunlight for photosynthesis is called what?
x: Chlorophyll, held in the chloroplasts, absorbs sunlight and uses it to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen.
e: Chlorophyll is green because it absorbs red and blue light and reflects green.

q: Which tissue carries water from the roots to the leaves of a plant?
x: Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals upwards from the roots. Phloem carries the food made in the leaves to the rest of the plant.
e: Xylem up with water; phloem around with food.

q: Nitrogen fixation in the root nodules of leguminous plants is carried out by which bacterium?
x: Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of pulses and other legumes and converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use, which is why pulses enrich the soil.
e: Rhizobium in the nodules of peas, grams and beans.

q: The system of binomial nomenclature for naming living things was given by whom?
x: Carolus Linnaeus introduced the two-part naming system in which each species gets a genus name and a species name, both written in Latin.
e: Two names: genus with a capital letter, species in lower case, both in italics.

q: Which is the largest mammal in the world?
x: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived, reaching about 30 metres and 150 tonnes. The African elephant is the largest land animal.
e: Biggest overall: blue whale. Biggest on land: African elephant.

q: The first UN Conference on the Human Environment, which led to World Environment Day, was held in 1972 in which city?
x: The Stockholm Conference of June 1972 was the first UN conference on the environment. It led to the creation of UNEP, and 5 June is marked as World Environment Day.
e: Stockholm 1972 → UNEP and World Environment Day on 5 June.

q: The Earth Summit of 1992, which produced the Convention on Biological Diversity, was held in which city?
x: The UN Conference on Environment and Development — the Earth Summit — was held at Rio de Janeiro in 1992. It produced Agenda 21, the UNFCCC and the Convention on Biological Diversity.
e: Rio 1992: Agenda 21, climate convention and biodiversity convention together.

q: Which was the first national park to be established in India?
x: Set up in 1936 as Hailey National Park in Uttarakhand, it was renamed Jim Corbett National Park and was the first national park in India. Project Tiger was launched there in 1973.
e: 1936 Hailey → Corbett; India's first national park and first tiger reserve.

q: Kaziranga National Park is famous for which animal?
x: Kaziranga in Assam holds the world's largest population of the Indian one-horned rhinoceros and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
e: Kaziranga rhino (Assam), Gir lion (Gujarat), Sundarbans tiger (West Bengal).

q: Which was the first biosphere reserve to be set up in India?
x: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, spread over Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, was notified in 1986 as India's first biosphere reserve.
e: Nilgiri 1986 — the first of India's biosphere reserves.

q: Project Tiger was launched in India in which year?
x: Project Tiger began in 1973 at Jim Corbett National Park, following the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972. Project Elephant came later, in 1992.
e: Act 1972, Project Tiger 1973, Project Elephant 1992.

q: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 deals with substances that damage what?
x: The Montreal Protocol controls the production and use of ozone-depleting substances such as chlorofluorocarbons. 16 September is observed as World Ozone Day.
e: Montreal ozone, Kyoto and Paris climate, Basel hazardous waste, Ramsar wetlands.

q: Excessive growth of algae in a water body caused by nutrient enrichment is called what?
x: Eutrophication happens when fertiliser run-off and sewage load a lake with nitrates and phosphates. The resulting algal bloom uses up dissolved oxygen and fish die.
e: Too many nutrients, too much algae, too little oxygen.

q: A high Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) in a sample of water indicates what?
o: The water is safe to drink
The water has a high mineral content
The water is highly polluted with organic matter
x: BOD measures the oxygen that micro-organisms need to break down the organic matter in water. The more organic pollution there is, the higher the BOD.
e: High BOD, dirty water; clean water has a low BOD.

q: The Ramsar Convention of 1971 deals with the conservation of what?
x: The Ramsar Convention, signed in Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, is the international treaty for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. 2 February is World Wetlands Day.
e: Ramsar = wetlands; Chilika was India's first Ramsar site.
